chunks.content: Once past acclimation, all of these aroids, and variegated forms especially, want a lot of light. Grow lights here sit very close to the plants and run twelve to fourteen hours a day, with the plants getting at least 250 PPFD and ideally 300 or more. Acclimating plantlets use a lower target of around 150 PPFD; see the acclimation protocol.
chunks.heading: Established plants: at least 250 PPFD for 12 to 14 hours

chunks.content: All established plants get at least 12 hours of light a day. Acclimating plantlets get 10 to 12, sometimes 12. The schedule is never shortened.
chunks.heading: Photoperiod used here

chunks.content: Big-box labels call tropical aroids medium- or low-light plants. Indoors, they almost never are. These are not outdoor plants unless they are slowly acclimated to sun, but as indoor plants they need more light than people think. Every aroid grown here is treated as a high-light plant with a target DLI of 15 or more, and established plants are given at least 250 PPFD, with 300 or more as the goal. Tissue-culture plantlets start lower, around 150 PPFD (it is not an exact figure), and pick up more light as they grow toward the fixture.
chunks.heading: Aroids are high-light plants, whatever the store label says

chunks.content: Alocasia are heavy feeders and need a lot of nutrients, plus consistent light. They also need very consistent watering and do not tolerate an irregular schedule the way a Monstera might. A self-watering setup is highly recommended for Alocasia to keep the watering consistent.
chunks.heading: Alocasia need consistent water, fertilizer, and light

chunks.content: Root growth is the main sign. With clear pots, visible roots mean things are going well. A second check when roots are not visible yet: tap the plant lightly, and if it feels more stable in the pot than before, it is rooting. Alocasia can drop every leaf during acclimation and people give up on them, but as long as the center of the plant, the rhizome, is still firm, keep it and keep watering; it will grow back.
chunks.heading: Signs acclimation is working

answer:
Right after potting, treat them as acclimating plantlets: aim for about 150 PPFD (not an exact figure, just a starting target) and run the light 10 to 12 hours a day. As they root in and start growing toward the fixture, you'll bump the light up, working toward the established-plant target of at least 250 PPFD (ideally 300+) on a 12 to 14 hour photoperiod.

On top of light, Alocasia are heavy feeders and need consistent watering and fertilizer too, they don't tolerate an irregular schedule well. A self-watering setup is recommended to keep that consistent. If they drop leaves during this stage, don't panic, that happens with Alocasia during acclimation, just check that the rhizome is still firm and keep watering.

chunks.content: A varied group of fertilizer products is used here and the brand does not matter. What matters is a 3-1-2 NPK ratio in any multiple: 6-2-4 and 9-3-6 are the same thing. If the fertilizer does not already include calcium and magnesium, add a cal-mag supplement. Dosing depends on the specific brand, so follow that product's label rather than a fixed rule; the standing practice is a light dose with every watering except the flush.
chunks.heading: Fertilizer: any 3-1-2 ratio, plus cal-mag

chunks.content: Alongside the IBA rooting hormone and Trichoderma T-22 in the first watering, Big Foot mycorrhizae and a "living charcoal" product are used: a biochar blended with natural fertilizers such as blood meal and worm castings. Exact brands vary and are hard to source consistently, so treat these as the categories to look for rather than specific products to buy.
chunks.heading: Rooting and biological products used here

chunks.content: For the first watering, per half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. That very small fertilizer dose in the first watering of the soil has resulted in success. Water the freshly potted plantlets with this once. After that, the next watering gets no fertilizer, and very light feeding starts with the watering after it. Under a 100 percent humidity dome it is usually at least ten days before they need water again.
chunks.heading: What goes in the first watering

chunks.content: Every watering carries a light dose of fertilizer, for all plants (tissue-culture plantlets skip it on their second watering), and this produced a large increase in growth. The other levers for a plant that has stalled are more light and a consistent routine.
chunks.heading: Light fertilizing with every watering

chunks.content: Past the first mix, plants move to a chunky aroid soil: coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera and Anthurium both love airflow around the roots; Monstera get the chunkiest version, and Anthurium a slightly less chunky one because their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle in a mix that is too chunky. A very large Alocasia with thick roots can eventually move to a chunkier mix, but that is far in the future.
chunks.heading: Second-stage mix after acclimation: chunky aroid soil

answer:
Use anything with a 3-1-2 NPK ratio (in any multiple, so 6-2-4 or 9-3-6 work the same way). Brand doesn't matter. If the product doesn't already include calcium and magnesium, add a cal-mag supplement on top. Dosing depends on the specific brand, so follow that product's label rather than a fixed rule, but the standing practice is a light dose with every watering except the flush.

For tissue-culture plantlets specifically, the first watering after potting gets a different mix: per half liter of water, one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. The next watering after that gets no fertilizer at all, and light feeding starts with the watering after that.

Once regular feeding starts, every watering carries a light dose of the 3-1-2 fertilizer for all plants (tissue-culture plantlets just skip it on their second watering). This light-every-time approach produced a large increase in growth. If a plant stalls, the other levers to pull are more light and a consistent routine.

chunks.content: Past the first mix, plants move to a chunky aroid soil: coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera and Anthurium both love airflow around the roots; Monstera get the chunkiest version, and Anthurium a slightly less chunky one because their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle in a mix that is too chunky. A very large Alocasia with thick roots can eventually move to a chunkier mix, but that is far in the future.
chunks.heading: Second-stage mix after acclimation: chunky aroid soil

chunks.content: The first potting mix for tissue-culture Monstera and Anthurium is tree fern fiber and perlite at about 45 percent each, plus about 10 percent coco coir. For Alocasia and Philodendron it is the same mix with about 20 percent coco coir, with the tree fern and perlite each dropping slightly to make room. The only goal of the change is a bit more dense material for fine roots to pull water from. Any plant with very fine, thin roots gets the denser mix, because fine roots need less airflow and need to be able to grab water from the substrate. A mix that is too dense is one of the most common beginner mistakes.
chunks.heading: First substrate mix by genus

chunks.content: Anthurium want lots of light and a chunky soil, but slightly thicker and not quite as chunky as the Monstera mix, because their roots start thinner. Do not let an Anthurium dry out as much as a Monstera.
chunks.heading: Anthurium substrate and watering

chunks.content: A varied group of fertilizer products is used here and the brand does not matter. What matters is a 3-1-2 NPK ratio in any multiple: 6-2-4 and 9-3-6 are the same thing. If the fertilizer does not already include calcium and magnesium, add a cal-mag supplement. Dosing depends on the specific brand, so follow that product's label rather than a fixed rule; the standing practice is a light dose with every watering except the flush.
chunks.heading: Fertilizer: any 3-1-2 ratio, plus cal-mag

chunks.content: Alongside the IBA rooting hormone and Trichoderma T-22 in the first watering, Big Foot mycorrhizae and a "living charcoal" product are used: a biochar blended with natural fertilizers such as blood meal and worm castings. Exact brands vary and are hard to source consistently, so treat these as the categories to look for rather than specific products to buy.
chunks.heading: Rooting and biological products used here

answer:
The right mix depends on the stage and the genus.

Right after acclimation, use tree fern fiber and perlite at about 45% each, plus about 10% coco coir for Monstera and Anthurium. For Alocasia and Philodendron, use the same mix but bump coco coir to about 20%, with the tree fern and perlite dropping slightly to make room for it. Their roots are finer and need more dense material to pull water from, but a mix that's too dense is one of the most common beginner mistakes, so don't overdo it.

Once plants move past that first stage, switch to a chunky aroid soil: coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera gets the chunkiest version. Anthurium gets a slightly less chunky version since its roots start out thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients but with more fine material and coco coir to hold water, since their finer roots struggle if the mix is too chunky. A very large Alocasia with thick roots can eventually move to a chunkier mix, but that's far off for a young plant.

For the first watering in that initial mix, IBA rooting hormone and Trichoderma T-22 are used, along with Big Foot mycorrhizae and a "living charcoal" product (a biochar blended with blood meal, worm castings, and similar natural fertilizers). Brands for these vary and can be hard to source consistently, so treat them as categories to look for rather than specific products to buy.

chunks.content: Alocasia stay at 100 percent humidity for about 15 to 20 days before the step-down starts, longer than a Monstera. Then, instead of reaching 65 percent humidity in about three weeks the way a Monstera does, an Alocasia takes four to five weeks to reach 65 percent. Once acclimated, an Alocasia is still not moved straight into ambient room humidity the way a Monstera can be; to bring one down to ambient humidity, give it a gradual acclimation like the one used for the tissue culture.
chunks.heading: Alocasia need a slower humidity step-down than Monstera

chunks.content: There is no single tell. Acclimation is done when the dome or lid can stay completely off and the plant is ready to move up a pot size. In a grow space held at 65 to 80 percent ambient humidity, stepping a Monstera down from 100 percent to 65 percent takes about three weeks, roughly 18 to 21 days, sometimes a little longer. Alocasia take four to five weeks. Anthurium and Philodendron sit in between. A drier room takes longer for all of them.
chunks.heading: When acclimation is done

chunks.content: Monstera are faster growers and more tolerant of problems than Alocasia or Anthurium. A Monstera reaches 65 percent humidity in about three weeks, roughly 18 to 21 days, sometimes a little longer. Once a Monstera is acclimated to 75 to 80 percent humidity and is more than a few inches tall, roughly in a three-inch pot, it can go straight into 50 percent humidity without issues. Alocasia need a much slower step-down and should not be moved like this.
chunks.heading: Monstera tolerate a faster humidity step-down

chunks.content: Alocasia lose leaves during acclimation very often. Most of the time new leaves replace the ones that drop. If the plant goes dormant instead, give it one to two months, sometimes longer, to show signs of growth or improvement before giving up, as long as the rhizome at the center stays firm.
chunks.heading: Leaf drop during Alocasia acclimation is normal

chunks.content: Philodendron sit between Monstera and Alocasia on humidity step-down: more time than a Monstera's three weeks, less than an Alocasia's four to five. They get a little longer than a Monstera specifically because their roots are thinner.
chunks.heading: Philodendron humidity step-down

answer:
Keep your Alocasia at 100 percent humidity for about 15 to 20 days before you start stepping the humidity down. After that, it takes another 4 to 5 weeks to get it down to 65 percent, which is slower than the roughly three weeks it takes a Monstera.

Once it's acclimated to 65 percent, don't move it straight into ambient room humidity. Bring it down gradually the same way you'd acclimate a fresh tissue culture plant.

Expect some leaf drop during this process, that's normal, and new leaves usually replace what's lost. If the plant goes dormant instead of pushing new growth, give it one to two months (sometimes longer) before giving up, as long as the rhizome in the center is still firm.

chunks.content: Every watering carries a light dose of fertilizer, for all plants (tissue-culture plantlets skip it on their second watering), and this produced a large increase in growth. The other levers for a plant that has stalled are more light and a consistent routine.
chunks.heading: Light fertilizing with every watering

chunks.content: Condensation and standing water under a dome are not something to worry about when planting tissue-culture plantlets. It goes away on its own as the dome is opened further during the humidity step-down.
chunks.heading: Condensation under domes is not a problem

chunks.content: This is for larger, established Anthurium, not for tissue-culture acclimation. Anthurium root from the base of the plant, so stacking a little moss over the soil around the root base, or adding a bit of soil there, gives those roots something to grow into and usually speeds up growth. Anthurium also do well climbing.
chunks.heading: Moss at the base speeds rooting on larger Anthurium

chunks.content: This is the one temperature rule that matters and most people do not know it: while plantlets are still sealed in the bag or flask, keep them below 75°F. If tissue-culture plantlets are being stored unplanted for a couple of days or longer, they must stay in a cooler spot, because in the bag they melt if it gets too hot. Once they are out of the bag and planted, ordinary room temperatures are fine.
chunks.heading: Unopened bags and flasks must stay below 75°F

chunks.content: For the first watering, per half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. That very small fertilizer dose in the first watering of the soil has resulted in success. Water the freshly potted plantlets with this once. After that, the next watering gets no fertilizer, and very light feeding starts with the watering after it. Under a 100 percent humidity dome it is usually at least ten days before they need water again.
chunks.heading: What goes in the first watering

answer:
For the very first watering, yes, but it's a specific mix, not a regular dose. Per half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. That tiny phosphorus dose in the first watering has worked well [general-substrate-water#what-goes-in-the-first-watering].

After that first watering, skip fertilizer entirely on the next watering, then start very light feeding from the watering after that [general-substrate-water#what-goes-in-the-first-watering]. Once you're into a normal routine, every watering after that carries a light dose of fertilizer for all plants, except tissue-culture plantlets still skip it on their second watering [general-substrate-water#light-fertilizing-with-every-watering].

Under a 100 percent humidity dome, expect at least ten days before the plantlets need water again after that first watering [general-substrate-water#what-goes-in-the-first-watering].

chunks.content: Spider mites are an easier kill than thrips. Neem oil, spinosad, or most other pesticide sprays work, combined with manually wiping the leaves. Wipe both sides of each leaf.
chunks.heading: Spider mites: sprays plus wiping

chunks.content: Thrips adapt to pesticides quickly and lay eggs in the soil, so treatment must be consistent and rotated between different pesticides. When thrips are found, spray every four days, mostly with a spinosad-based pesticide. Where it is legal, systemic granules (imidacloprid or a similar active ingredient) watered into the soil protect the plant for a month or more; the plant takes the chemical up and pests that bite it die. Do not use systemic granules if spider mites are present: they have been found to speed up spider-mite reproduction rather than kill them, so an infestation can spread faster.
chunks.heading: Thrips: rotate sprays every four days, or use systemic granules

chunks.content: Any premixed potting soil or similar product should be treated for fungus gnats immediately on first use, before an infestation starts. The method: soak Mosquito Bits (the brand) in the water you are about to water with for a few hours, then water with it. This kills the larvae in the soil far more efficiently than the usual published methods like spraying oil on the surface or covering the top of the soil.
chunks.heading: Fungus gnats: treat premixed soil the day you use it

chunks.content: Alocasia tend to attract more pests than other genera. When pests are found on an Alocasia, treat for longer than you would treat a Monstera, and keep watching the plant closely afterward to confirm nothing new has arrived. The pest protocols themselves (thrips, spider mites, mealybugs) are the same as for other aroids.
chunks.heading: Alocasia attract more pests and get treated longer

chunks.content: Cut off the affected leaves immediately, even if it is the plant's only leaf, and spray with a copper fungicide. A fungicide can also be applied while watering. If leaf spot keeps recurring, add more airflow to the setup. Isolate the plant if it sits near other Alocasia, and treat the surrounding plants with a fungicide as well, exactly as you would for a pest outbreak.
chunks.heading: Leaf spot on Alocasia: what to do

answer:
Thrips are tougher to kill than spider mites because they adapt to pesticides fast and lay eggs down in the soil, so you have to stay consistent and rotate products rather than spraying once and stopping.

When you find thrips, spray every four days, mostly with a spinosad-based pesticide. Where it's legal, you can also water in systemic granules (imidacloprid or similar) — the plant takes the chemical up through its system and it kills pests that bite it, giving protection for a month or more.

One catch: don't use systemic granules if you've also got spider mites on the plant. Granules have been shown to speed up spider-mite reproduction instead of killing them, so that infestation would spread faster.

If this is an Alocasia specifically, treat it longer than you would a Monstera and keep watching it closely afterward, since Alocasia tend to attract more pests overall — but the actual thrips treatment steps above are the same across aroid genera.

chunks.content: When plantlets arrive, do not open the bag. Let them sit sealed for a day or two in the spot where they will be grown, so they adjust to that room's temperature and light before anything else changes.
chunks.heading: Day 0 to day 2: leave them sealed

chunks.content: This is the one temperature rule that matters and most people do not know it: while plantlets are still sealed in the bag or flask, keep them below 75°F. If tissue-culture plantlets are being stored unplanted for a couple of days or longer, they must stay in a cooler spot, because in the bag they melt if it gets too hot. Once they are out of the bag and planted, ordinary room temperatures are fine.
chunks.heading: Unopened bags and flasks must stay below 75°F

chunks.content: At week one the plantlet should look about the same as when it was potted, just a little perkier. A plant that flopped because it grew crooked in the bag is fine as long as it feels firm in the pot. A plant that moves around a lot when touched needs checking.
chunks.heading: What a TC Monstera should look like at week one

chunks.content: Water once at potting. Because humidity sits at 100 percent under the dome, it is usually at least ten days before the plantlets need water again.
chunks.heading: Watering cadence under the dome

chunks.content: Condensation and standing water under a dome are not something to worry about when planting tissue-culture plantlets. It goes away on its own as the dome is opened further during the humidity step-down.
chunks.heading: Condensation under domes is not a problem

answer:
No, not if it's hot where you are. While plantlets are still sealed in the bag, they need to stay below 75°F — if it's warmer than that and they sit unplanted for a couple of days or more, they'll melt in the bag. Find a cooler spot to keep them sealed until you can pot them up. Once you pot them and get them under a dome, room temperature is fine.

When they do arrive, don't open the bag right away either — let them sit sealed for a day or two in the room where they'll be grown so they adjust before you do anything else, as long as that room stays under 75°F.

chunks.content: Thai Constellation, albo, aurea, white monster, and the other variegated Monstera all get the same treatment; there is no real care difference between them. They all get a lot of light, placed in the strongest spot under the bar, to fight reversion and grow quickly.
chunks.heading: All variegated Monstera get the same light and care

chunks.content: No single Alocasia is grown here more than the others. Some are more sensitive and slower-growing than others, but every Alocasia gets the same materials and protocol. An extremely expensive plant gets more consistent watching and care, but nothing about the substrate, water, or schedule changes.
chunks.heading: All Alocasia get the same treatment

chunks.content: Tissue-culture Monstera here are mostly Monstera deliciosa and Monstera borsigiana, and almost all variegated: Thai Constellation, albo, white monster, bulbosa, devil monster, green on green, aurea, and many more. All of them are handled the same way. Monstera adansonii has not been grown from tissue culture here, so nothing in this corpus covers it.
chunks.heading: Which Monstera this covers

chunks.content: Anthurium are more humidity-sensitive than Monstera. Their step-down gets more time than a Monstera and less time than an Alocasia, sitting right between the two. Otherwise they get the same protocol as a Monstera.
chunks.heading: Anthurium humidity step-down sits between Monstera and Alocasia

chunks.content: Alocasia tend to attract more pests than other genera. When pests are found on an Alocasia, treat for longer than you would treat a Monstera, and keep watching the plant closely afterward to confirm nothing new has arrived. The pest protocols themselves (thrips, spider mites, mealybugs) are the same as for other aroids.
chunks.heading: Alocasia attract more pests and get treated longer

answer: No. Thai Constellation, albo, aurea, white monster, and the other variegated Monstera all get the same treatment. There's no real care difference between them. All of them go in the strongest light spot under the bar to fight reversion and grow quickly.

chunks.content: The Barrina T5 is the most common cheap grow light customers own. It is full spectrum, but a single bar puts out very little usable light and it falls off fast with distance. Per its product chart, measured at the center of the bar, one bar delivers about 91 PPFD at 8 inches, 59.3 at 12 inches, and 31.2 at 20 inches. At 8 inches, which is quite close, for 12 hours a day, that is a DLI of 3.93, below even the low-light band. To make a T5 setup work, stack several bars side by side or buy a stronger fixture.
chunks.heading: The Barrina T5 is weak: the numbers

chunks.content: Usable light drops off with distance from the fixture far faster than people expect. On a single Barrina T5, the product chart shows 91 PPFD at 8 inches, 59.3 at 12 inches, and 31.2 at 20 inches. It also drops toward the ends of a bar compared with directly under its center. Cheaper fixtures and cheaper LED nodes make both effects worse.
chunks.heading: Light intensity drops off fast with distance

chunks.content: Once past acclimation, all of these aroids, and variegated forms especially, want a lot of light. Grow lights here sit very close to the plants and run twelve to fourteen hours a day, with the plants getting at least 250 PPFD and ideally 300 or more. Acclimating plantlets use a lower target of around 150 PPFD; see the acclimation protocol.
chunks.heading: Established plants: at least 250 PPFD for 12 to 14 hours

chunks.content: Light intensity and fixture distance depend on the light, so the target is the reading, not the distance: around 150 PPFD (not an exact figure) for about ten to twelve hours a day, versus at least 250 for established plants. As the plantlets grow taller they get closer to the fixture, which raises their light exposure on its own and matches their growing need for light, so there is no need to turn the light up.
chunks.heading: Light: around 150 PPFD for 10 to 12 hours

chunks.content: There is no single tell. Acclimation is done when the dome or lid can stay completely off and the plant is ready to move up a pot size. In a grow space held at 65 to 80 percent ambient humidity, stepping a Monstera down from 100 percent to 65 percent takes about three weeks, roughly 18 to 21 days, sometimes a little longer. Alocasia take four to five weeks. Anthurium and Philodendron sit in between. A drier room takes longer for all of them.
chunks.heading: When acclimation is done

answer:
At 8 inches for 12 hours, one Barrina T5 bar gives you about 91 PPFD at the center, which works out to a DLI of 3.93 — that's below even the low-light band [general-light-hardware#the-barrina-t5-is-weak-the-numbers].

That's not enough for a Monstera albo either as an acclimating plantlet or as an established plant. Acclimating plantlets want around 150 PPFD for 10-12 hours a day, and established plants (variegated forms especially) want at least 250 PPFD, ideally 300+, for 12-14 hours [general-acclimation#light-around-150-ppfd-for-10-to-12-hours][general-light#established-plants-at-least-250-ppfd-for-12-to-14-hours].

A single T5 bar just doesn't put out enough usable light, and it falls off fast with distance — moving it closer than 8 inches won't get you there. To fix this, stack several bars side by side or switch to a stronger fixture [general-light-hardware#the-barrina-t5-is-weak-the-numbers][general-light#light-intensity-drops-off-fast-with-distance].

chunks.content: Water once at potting. Because humidity sits at 100 percent under the dome, it is usually at least ten days before the plantlets need water again.
chunks.heading: Watering cadence under the dome

chunks.content: Starting humidity is always 100 percent, either a single pot under its own dome or a tray with a dome. Hold 100 percent for at least a week. After about a week, start opening the vents or lifting the lid slightly and keep stepping the humidity down slowly from there. Both directions of error hurt: stepping down too slowly delays growth because the plant needs airflow and lower humidity to keep acclimating, and stepping down too fast, or never giving 100 percent at the start, kills plantlets.
chunks.heading: Humidity: hold 100 percent for the first week

chunks.content: After planting from tissue culture, leaves sometimes melt away: they turn to mush and die off. This is pretty common. As long as the base of the plant is fine (the base, not a leaf's stalk), keep taking care of it. If leaves are turning to mush, consider a slight change to watering, because you might be overwatering, and add some daily airflow if you can. Early in the stage, even opening the dome slightly for a few minutes gets fresh air in.
chunks.heading: Leaves melting away after planting is common

chunks.content: Condensation and standing water under a dome are not something to worry about when planting tissue-culture plantlets. It goes away on its own as the dome is opened further during the humidity step-down.
chunks.heading: Condensation under domes is not a problem

chunks.content: Once a plant is past the dome and not on a wick, it is top watered. Water until a little runs out of the bottom of the pot every time, so the whole pot is evenly saturated, then let it drain fully. Do not leave it soaked; the goal is a complete, even watering, not a heavy one.
chunks.heading: Top watering after the dome: water until it drains

answer:
Start at 100 percent humidity under the dome, and hold that for at least a week. After about a week, start opening the vents or lifting the lid slightly, then keep stepping humidity down slowly from there. Don't rush it and don't skip the initial 100 percent — going too fast or too slow both hurt the plantlets, with too fast/no initial dome time actually killing them. If you see condensation or standing water under the dome, that's normal and clears up on its own as you open it further during step-down.

On watering: you water once at potting, and because humidity is 100 percent under the dome, it's usually at least ten days before they need water again. If leaves melt to mush during this stage, that's common — as long as the base of the plant is fine, keep going, and consider watering less and adding some daily airflow (even cracking the dome for a few minutes helps).

I don't have information on that in my notes when it comes to a feeding/fertilizing schedule.

chunks.content: Leaves yellowing right after a plant comes out from under the humidity dome are most likely a humidity problem rather than a light problem, usually from taking the dome off too fast. Also make sure the soil is not drying out too much or staying too damp.
chunks.heading: Yellowing leaves once the dome comes off

chunks.content: A plant that seems to be leaning away from the light, or develops a yellowish burned area on the leaf, is getting light burn, the indoor version of sunburn. Fixtures can also run hot, and a leaf touching a hot fixture will burn; it has not happened here but it can.
chunks.heading: Signs of too much light

chunks.content: After planting from tissue culture, leaves sometimes melt away: they turn to mush and die off. This is pretty common. As long as the base of the plant is fine (the base, not a leaf's stalk), keep taking care of it. If leaves are turning to mush, consider a slight change to watering, because you might be overwatering, and add some daily airflow if you can. Early in the stage, even opening the dome slightly for a few minutes gets fresh air in.
chunks.heading: Leaves melting away after planting is common

chunks.content: Root rot is the main problem across all genera, especially while plants are small and held in high humidity. The cause is almost always too little airflow under the dome or lid. With Alocasia, watch for fungus as well, for the same reason: give them a good amount of airflow. On an established plant, rot looks the same as overwatering: yellowing, wilting, droopiness, browning edges, and mushy sections. Directly after planting from tissue culture the only early sign is usually a loss of firmness, and by the time leaves die it is too late.
chunks.heading: Root rot is the biggest risk for small plants

chunks.content: Water once at potting. Because humidity sits at 100 percent under the dome, it is usually at least ten days before the plantlets need water again.
chunks.heading: Watering cadence under the dome

answer: It's most likely a humidity problem, not light. Yellowing right after the dome comes off usually happens because the dome was removed too fast. Check that the soil isn't drying out too much or staying too damp, since that can compound the issue.

chunks.content: Monstera are faster growers and more tolerant of problems than Alocasia or Anthurium. A Monstera reaches 65 percent humidity in about three weeks, roughly 18 to 21 days, sometimes a little longer. Once a Monstera is acclimated to 75 to 80 percent humidity and is more than a few inches tall, roughly in a three-inch pot, it can go straight into 50 percent humidity without issues. Alocasia need a much slower step-down and should not be moved like this.
chunks.heading: Monstera tolerate a faster humidity step-down

chunks.content: There is no single tell. Acclimation is done when the dome or lid can stay completely off and the plant is ready to move up a pot size. In a grow space held at 65 to 80 percent ambient humidity, stepping a Monstera down from 100 percent to 65 percent takes about three weeks, roughly 18 to 21 days, sometimes a little longer. Alocasia take four to five weeks. Anthurium and Philodendron sit in between. A drier room takes longer for all of them.
chunks.heading: When acclimation is done

chunks.content: Past the first mix, plants move to a chunky aroid soil: coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera and Anthurium both love airflow around the roots; Monstera get the chunkiest version, and Anthurium a slightly less chunky one because their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle in a mix that is too chunky. A very large Alocasia with thick roots can eventually move to a chunkier mix, but that is far in the future.
chunks.heading: Second-stage mix after acclimation: chunky aroid soil

chunks.content: The first potting mix for tissue-culture Monstera and Anthurium is tree fern fiber and perlite at about 45 percent each, plus about 10 percent coco coir. For Alocasia and Philodendron it is the same mix with about 20 percent coco coir, with the tree fern and perlite each dropping slightly to make room. The only goal of the change is a bit more dense material for fine roots to pull water from. Any plant with very fine, thin roots gets the denser mix, because fine roots need less airflow and need to be able to grab water from the substrate. A mix that is too dense is one of the most common beginner mistakes.
chunks.heading: First substrate mix by genus

chunks.content: No new growth or undersized leaves on a Monstera almost always means not enough fertilizer and not enough light. Variegated Monstera in particular want a lot of light. The questions to ask first: how consistent is the watering and fertilizing routine, what light is the plant under, and how far from it is the plant.
chunks.heading: No new growth or small leaves on Monstera

answer:
For a tissue-culture Monstera, the first potting mix is tree fern fiber and perlite at about 45 percent each, plus about 10 percent coco coir [general-substrate-water#first-substrate-mix-by-genus]. That mix is meant to give plenty of airflow around the roots, since Monstera do best with a chunky, airy setup [general-substrate-water#second-stage-mix-after-acclimation-chunky-aroid-soil]. Once acclimated and past a few inches tall (around a three-inch pot), it moves to a chunkier aroid soil of coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark, with Monstera getting the chunkiest version of that mix [general-substrate-water#second-stage-mix-after-acclimation-chunky-aroid-soil].

I don't have information on how wet to keep the substrate during those first couple weeks.

chunks.content: Bugs are not common while plantlets are still under the dome, and what to do depends on the bug. Most likely it is springtails or soil mites; if so, leave them, because they are beneficial. A harmful pest such as thrips or spider mites must be treated, along with all the plants around it, but plantlets are extremely fragile at that stage, which puts you in a difficult position. A plantlet cannot be sprayed and then put under grow lights: it will most likely burn and die. Spray gently at night so the leaves can dry off.
chunks.heading: Bugs under the dome: leave springtails, treat pests gently at night

chunks.content: After planting from tissue culture, leaves sometimes melt away: they turn to mush and die off. This is pretty common. As long as the base of the plant is fine (the base, not a leaf's stalk), keep taking care of it. If leaves are turning to mush, consider a slight change to watering, because you might be overwatering, and add some daily airflow if you can. Early in the stage, even opening the dome slightly for a few minutes gets fresh air in.
chunks.heading: Leaves melting away after planting is common

chunks.content: Water once at potting. Because humidity sits at 100 percent under the dome, it is usually at least ten days before the plantlets need water again.
chunks.heading: Watering cadence under the dome

chunks.content: Condensation and standing water under a dome are not something to worry about when planting tissue-culture plantlets. It goes away on its own as the dome is opened further during the humidity step-down.
chunks.heading: Condensation under domes is not a problem

chunks.content: Cut off the affected leaves immediately, even if it is the plant's only leaf, and spray with a copper fungicide. A fungicide can also be applied while watering. If leaf spot keeps recurring, add more airflow to the setup. Isolate the plant if it sits near other Alocasia, and treat the surrounding plants with a fungicide as well, exactly as you would for a pest outbreak.
chunks.heading: Leaf spot on Alocasia: what to do

answer:
It depends on what the bug is. Bugs under the dome aren't common in the first place, but if you're seeing them, most likely it's springtails or soil mites, and if so, leave them alone since they're beneficial.

If it's a harmful pest like thrips or spider mites, you do need to treat it, along with all the plants around it, but plantlets at this stage are extremely fragile. Spraying a plantlet and then putting it back under grow lights will most likely burn and kill it. So spray gently at night instead, so the leaves have time to dry off before any light exposure.

chunks.content: The grow tents run either AC Infinity S16 light bars, which use Samsung LED diodes and carry light much further down so it dissipates more slowly, or the thicker Barrina TXS45A bars. AC Infinity does not publish PPFD figures, and the S16 can be set to multiple levels, so its output is hard to judge. Its bars use Samsung LM301H EVO LEDs, rated at 3.14 µmol/J PPE, and a set of four IONBEAM S16 bars is listed at 42 watts. The Barrina TXS45A listing (135 W, three 45 W bars, CRI 98) shows, per light and measured at the center of the bar, 429.7 PPFD at 3.94 inches, 216.9 at 7.87 inches, and 137 at 11.81 inches, which is about 2.4 times a Barrina T5 at the same 8-inch distance. A few inches from the plants these fixtures deliver roughly 350 PPFD, which over 12 hours is a DLI of about 15. That is too much for a very small plant, but small plants are easy to set further from the fixture, and as they grow they move closer and their PPFD rises on its own.
chunks.heading: The stronger fixtures used here

chunks.content: AC Infinity publishes no PPFD chart for the S16, so its light is estimated from power. A set of four IONBEAM S16 bars draws 42 watts at level 10, and power scales with the level: about 29.4 watts at level 7 and 21 watts at level 5. Multiplying the watts by the LM301H EVO rating of 3.14 µmol/J gives the light the bars put out: about 132 µmol/s at level 10, 92 at level 7, and 66 at level 5. Dividing that by the lit area in square meters gives the average PPFD across the area: over a 2 × 2 ft space (0.37 m²) about 355 at level 10, 248 at level 7, and 177 at level 5; over a 2 × 4 ft space (0.74 m²) about 177, 124, and 89. These are estimates from the LED rating, not measurements, and they are averages across the whole area, while the Barrina charts measure the center of the bar, where light is strongest.
chunks.heading: Estimating AC Infinity S16 light from its watts

chunks.content: Once past acclimation, all of these aroids, and variegated forms especially, want a lot of light. Grow lights here sit very close to the plants and run twelve to fourteen hours a day, with the plants getting at least 250 PPFD and ideally 300 or more. Acclimating plantlets use a lower target of around 150 PPFD; see the acclimation protocol.
chunks.heading: Established plants: at least 250 PPFD for 12 to 14 hours

chunks.content: All established plants get at least 12 hours of light a day. Acclimating plantlets get 10 to 12, sometimes 12. The schedule is never shortened.
chunks.heading: Photoperiod used here

chunks.content: Light intensity and fixture distance depend on the light, so the target is the reading, not the distance: around 150 PPFD (not an exact figure) for about ten to twelve hours a day, versus at least 250 for established plants. As the plantlets grow taller they get closer to the fixture, which raises their light exposure on its own and matches their growing need for light, so there is no need to turn the light up.
chunks.heading: Light: around 150 PPFD for 10 to 12 hours

answer:
AC Infinity doesn't publish a PPFD chart for the S16, so there's no way to tell you the exact reading at 10 inches [general-light-hardware#the-stronger-fixtures-used-here]. What you can do instead is estimate from the wattage: a set of four IONBEAM S16 bars draws 42 watts at level 10, about 29.4 watts at level 7, and 21 watts at level 5, and multiplying watts by the LM301H EVO rating of 3.14 µmol/J gives roughly 132, 92, and 66 µmol/s at those levels. Divide that by your lit area in square meters to get average PPFD: over a 2×2 ft space that's about 355 at level 10, 248 at level 7, 177 at level 5; over a 2×4 ft space about 177, 124, 89 [general-light-hardware#estimating-ac-infinity-s16-light-from-its-watts]. These are estimates from the LED rating, not actual measurements, and they're averages across the whole lit area rather than a distance-based figure, so they won't tell you precisely what's hitting the plant at 10 inches.

On timing, 14 hours a day is fine and won't need shortening [general-light-hardware#photoperiod-used-here]. For established philodendrons past acclimation, the target is at least 250 PPFD and ideally 300+, run 12 to 14 hours a day [general-light#established-plants-at-least-250-ppfd-for-12-to-14-hours]. Check which level your S16 is set to and estimate PPFD from the numbers above for your tent size — if it's coming in under 250, move the light closer or bump the level up.

chunks.content: Root growth is the main sign. With clear pots, visible roots mean things are going well. A second check when roots are not visible yet: tap the plant lightly, and if it feels more stable in the pot than before, it is rooting. Alocasia can drop every leaf during acclimation and people give up on them, but as long as the center of the plant, the rhizome, is still firm, keep it and keep watering; it will grow back.
chunks.heading: Signs acclimation is working

chunks.content: Alocasia are heavy feeders and need a lot of nutrients, plus consistent light. They also need very consistent watering and do not tolerate an irregular schedule the way a Monstera might. A self-watering setup is highly recommended for Alocasia to keep the watering consistent.
chunks.heading: Alocasia need consistent water, fertilizer, and light

chunks.content: Alocasia lose leaves during acclimation very often. Most of the time new leaves replace the ones that drop. If the plant goes dormant instead, give it one to two months, sometimes longer, to show signs of growth or improvement before giving up, as long as the rhizome at the center stays firm.
chunks.heading: Leaf drop during Alocasia acclimation is normal

chunks.content: Alocasia are dramatic: droopy leaves and leaves dying one after another are the most common customer complaint, and it is usually an overreaction. A small Alocasia normally cannot hold more than a couple of leaves. While small, it will typically grow one new leaf while the older leaf dies at the same time, so the plant sits at one leaf. Give it time; as the root system gets stronger and the plant gets bigger it will hold more leaves.
chunks.heading: Droopy or dying leaves on a small Alocasia

chunks.content: Root rot is the main problem across all genera, especially while plants are small and held in high humidity. The cause is almost always too little airflow under the dome or lid. With Alocasia, watch for fungus as well, for the same reason: give them a good amount of airflow. On an established plant, rot looks the same as overwatering: yellowing, wilting, droopiness, browning edges, and mushy sections. Directly after planting from tissue culture the only early sign is usually a loss of firmness, and by the time leaves die it is too late.
chunks.heading: Root rot is the biggest risk for small plants

chunks.content: Tissue-culture Monstera here are mostly Monstera deliciosa and Monstera borsigiana, and almost all variegated: Thai Constellation, albo, white monster, bulbosa, devil monster, green on green, aurea, and many more. All of them are handled the same way. Monstera adansonii has not been grown from tissue culture here, so nothing in this corpus covers it.

chunks.content: Big-box labels call tropical aroids medium- or low-light plants. Indoors, they almost never are. These are not outdoor plants unless they are slowly acclimated to sun, but as indoor plants they need more light than people think. Every aroid grown here is treated as a high-light plant with a target DLI of 15 or more, and established plants are given at least 250 PPFD, with 300 or more as the goal. Tissue-culture plantlets start lower, around 150 PPFD (it is not an exact figure), and pick up more light as they grow toward the fixture.
chunks.heading: Aroids are high-light plants, whatever the store label says

chunks.content: Brown tips and slow growth are the Anthurium questions customers ask most, and they are normally a humidity and watering issue. The common mistake is giving an Anthurium too little light and treating it as fussily as an Alocasia. Anthurium are not as dramatic as Alocasia and hold up well; the one thing to guard is never letting them dry out completely.
chunks.heading: Brown tips and slow growth on Anthurium

chunks.content: Once past acclimation, all of these aroids, and variegated forms especially, want a lot of light. Grow lights here sit very close to the plants and run twelve to fourteen hours a day, with the plants getting at least 250 PPFD and ideally 300 or more. Acclimating plantlets use a lower target of around 150 PPFD; see the acclimation protocol.
chunks.heading: Established plants: at least 250 PPFD for 12 to 14 hours

chunks.content: Anthurium want lots of light and a chunky soil, but slightly thicker and not quite as chunky as the Monstera mix, because their roots start thinner. Do not let an Anthurium dry out as much as a Monstera.
chunks.heading: Anthurium substrate and watering

chunks.content: This is for larger, established Anthurium, not for tissue-culture acclimation. Anthurium root from the base of the plant, so stacking a little moss over the soil around the root base, or adding a bit of soil there, gives those roots something to grow into and usually speeds up growth. Anthurium also do well climbing.
chunks.heading: Moss at the base speeds rooting on larger Anthurium

chunks.content: Condensation and standing water under a dome are not something to worry about when planting tissue-culture plantlets. It goes away on its own as the dome is opened further during the humidity step-down.

chunks.content: This is the one temperature rule that matters and most people do not know it: while plantlets are still sealed in the bag or flask, keep them below 75°F. If tissue-culture plantlets are being stored unplanted for a couple of days or longer, they must stay in a cooler spot, because in the bag they melt if it gets too hot. Once they are out of the bag and planted, ordinary room temperatures are fine.
chunks.heading: Unopened bags and flasks must stay below 75°F

chunks.content: A variety of Philodendron are grown from tissue culture here. The most common is Philodendron Caramel Marble, along with its pink form, sold as Pink Caramel Marble or Strawberry Philodendron, which is a slightly separate plant. These are very slow growers.
chunks.heading: Which Philodendron this covers

chunks.content: Philodendron are treated much the same as Monstera. Both are hardy. Philodendron can dry out, can take low humidity, and are resilient to changes in conditions.
chunks.heading: Philodendron are hardy and treated like Monstera

chunks.content: Slow growth is the Philodendron question customers ask most, and most of the time it is simply how the plant grows: Philodendron, and Caramel Marble types especially, are very slow growers. It is the main thing customers get confused about with Philodendron and Anthurium.
chunks.heading: Slow growth on Philodendron is usually normal

chunks.content: There are no pests or fungal problems specific to Philodendron. They are treated the same as a Monstera: manual wiping, consistent spraying, and regular checking, following the general thrips, spider mite, and mealybug protocols.
chunks.heading: No Philodendron-specific pests or fungus

chunks.content: Philodendron are the slowest rooters of the four genera. Monstera are fastest, Anthurium and Alocasia are second, Philodendron last. Philodendron also do well climbing.
chunks.heading: Philodendron root the slowest

Isolate the plant if it sits near other Alocasia, and treat the surrounding plants with a fungicide as well, exactly as you would for a pest outbreak.

chunks.content: First: overdoing the start. Distilled water, extra coatings, hormones, and fertilizer on top of each other are not needed, and success rates were higher cleaning the plantlets off under plain running water at the sink. Second: mistiming the humidity step-down, either dragging it out (delayed growth, the plant needs airflow) or yanking the dome off or never starting at 100 percent (kills the plant). Third: potting into a soil that is too dense.
chunks.heading: Mistakes beginners make most

chunks.content: Yellowing and black spots on a Monstera are most often root rot. Root rot is the biggest issue for small plants held in high humidity without enough airflow.
chunks.heading: Yellowing leaves or black spots on Monstera

chunks.content: Every cabinet and grow area has a light fan to fight fungus and mold. It does not need to be strong: leaves should not be whipping around. The test is slight movement in some leaves, or a little movement in the fabric wall of a grow tent. That is enough to keep the air from going still and stale around the plants, which is what causes fungal problems. When fungus shows up anywhere, airflow is one of the first things to check.
chunks.heading: Every grow area has a light fan running

chunks.content: For a customer whose house sits around 40 percent humidity: group plants together so they raise the humidity around each other, consider a cabinet with light bars for both humidity and light, and when a new plant first arrives, cover it in a clear plastic bag and slowly expose it to more air over time so it adjusts to the room's ambient humidity instead of being shocked by it.
chunks.heading: Advice for a dry home with no cabinet

chunks.content: Oil-based sprays, homemade or store-bought, work on mealybugs. Removing them by hand with a rubbing-alcohol swab is very effective and easy.
chunks.heading: Mealybugs: oil sprays and alcohol swabs

Monstera and Anthurium both love airflow around the roots; Monstera get the chunkiest version, and Anthurium a slightly less chunky one because their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle in a mix that is too chunky. A very large Alocasia with thick roots can eventually move to a chunkier mix, but that is far in the future.

chunks.content: Thai Constellation, albo, aurea, white monster, and the other variegated Monstera all get the same treatment; there is no real care difference between them. They all get a lot of light, placed in the strongest spot under the bar, to fight reversion and grow quickly.
chunks.heading: All variegated Monstera get the same light and care

chunks.content: Alocasia tend to attract more pests than other genera. When pests are found on an Alocasia, treat for longer than you would treat a Monstera, and keep watching the plant closely afterward to confirm nothing new has arrived. The pest protocols themselves (thrips, spider mites, mealybugs) are the same as for other aroids.
chunks.heading: Alocasia attract more pests and get treated longer

chunks.content: A light bar is strongest directly under its center and weaker toward its ends, so PPFD drops as you move a plant toward the sides. The most light-hungry plants go in the center: variegated Monstera and Alocasia get the most light here. Anything that wants less light, or is getting too much under a strong fixture, goes toward the side or further away.
chunks.heading: Where to put each plant under a bar

chunks.content: Water once at potting. Because humidity sits at 100 percent under the dome, it is usually at least ten days before the plantlets need water again.
chunks.heading: Watering cadence under the dome

chunks.content: For the first watering, per half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. That very small fertilizer dose in the first watering of the soil has resulted in success. Water the freshly potted plantlets with this once. After that, the next watering gets no fertilizer, and very light feeding starts with the watering after it. Under a 100 percent humidity dome it is usually at least ten days before they need water again.
chunks.heading: What goes in the first watering

chunks.content: DLI (daily light integral) is PPFD multiplied by the hours the light is on, so it captures how much light a plant gets over a whole day rather than at one instant. Addition (standard formula, matches the Waveform Lighting DLI calculator at waveformlighting.com/horticulture/daily-light-integral-dli-calculator): DLI = PPFD × hours × 3600 ÷ 1,000,000. By that calculator's bands, low-light plants need a DLI of 5 to 10, medium-light plants 10 to 15, and high-light plants more than 15.
chunks.heading: What DLI means and the three light bands

chunks.content: By week three there should be multiple visible roots in a clear pot, or at least one piece of new growth, often a couple. In a one-and-a-half-inch starter pot this is usually up-pot time; in a larger pot it will not be yet.
chunks.heading: What a TC Monstera should look like at week three

chunks.content: A varied group of fertilizer products is used here and the brand does not matter. What matters is a 3-1-2 NPK ratio in any multiple: 6-2-4 and 9-3-6 are the same thing. If the fertilizer does not already include calcium and magnesium, add a cal-mag supplement. Dosing depends on the specific brand, so follow that product's label rather than a fixed rule; the standing practice is a light dose with every watering except the flush.
chunks.heading: Fertilizer: any 3-1-2 ratio, plus cal-mag
